persp-name-globe: Observer's perspective — solid = globe, dashed = flat
persp-name-flat: Observer's perspective — solid = flat, dashed = globe
water-cut: water out to the horizon at {v} — the globe buries everything below this line
water-cut-near: water out to the horizon at {v} — the target is nearer, so it stands in front of it
persp-meta-zoom: · vertical ×{v} — not a true photo scale
status-grazing: top visible, base hidden by curve
sizes-note: The peaks change size by at most {worstSize}% between the two models — a fraction of an arcsecond, far below what any lens or eye resolves. But they change position relative to eye level by up to {worstPos}′, hundreds of times larger. That is the whole reason this test works with a level and a protractor rather than a camera: the curve barely distorts what things look like, it moves where they sit. Anyone claiming “the mountains look normal, so it's flat” is checking the quantity the two models agree on.
re-needtwo: Needs at least two targets at different distances.
re-row-measured-obs-note: — the reading both methods start from
re-row-diverge-note: ✗ the rays truly diverge by only {v}′ — overstated {x}×
re-ht-sines: Law of sines (allows level to tilt by b/R)
re-ht-sines-no-br: Law of sines without b/R (flat surveyor's version)
re-flat-diff-note: the entire signal the method works from
re-flat-share: b/R as a share of that difference
re-flat-share-note: the correction is {cmp} the signal itself
re-flat-truediv: True divergence of the two rays
re-flat-note: Because the sine rule divides by the divergence, overstating it {x}× collapses the distance: the flat surveyor concludes the summit stands {near} away instead of {far}. That is the whole argument in one number — you can drive there and find an empty field. No globe was assumed anywhere: it uses only the flat‑Earther's own two angle readings, their own baseline, and their own trigonometry. The method refutes itself.
re-note: Baseline b = {b}. Both methods read the same two real angles, so both agree the summit sits below eye level — the globe's answer, not the flat model's {flat}′. The split appears in the height: on a genuine plane the tangent and law-of-sines formulas are algebraically the same, so they must return the same number. Here they differ by {diff} m. That disagreement is only possible if the two “level” references are not parallel — which is curvature, measured.
recip-row-zA: Zenith angle at the observer, z_A
recip-row-sum-note: what the two instruments actually total
recip-row-flat-note: ✗ exact, for any distance and any heights
recip-row-radius: Earth radius from the excess, R = d/(sum−180°)
recip-note: The two readings miss 180° by {v}′. That excess is not an error bar — it is d/R, the same angle by which the two protractors' 0° lines are tilted in the figure above, and the same b/R the flat two‑station method drops in section 04. Note what is not in the flat prediction: no distance, no height, no instrument constant. It is 180° or the Earth is not flat.
why-line2: FLAT  {flat}  vs  GLOBE {globe}  →  {diff} apart (a full moon spans 31′)
why-flip: The two models disagree about the sign: the plane puts it above eye level, the globe below. No instrument error and no calibration dispute can turn a + into a −.
why-level: This target is at exactly the observer's own height, so the plane puts it at exactly 0.0000° — dead level, by definition, at any distance. The globe puts it {v}. That is the cleanest form of the test: no height difference to argue about.
why-amount: Same side of eye level in both models, so this one is decided by the amount — {v}′ is {x} full-moon widths.
why-horizon-allin: — every target is inside it, so “too far to see” is not available to either side.
why-horizon-some: — {n} of the {total} {verb} beyond it, which the flat model has no way to express at all: a plane has no horizon.
results-note: From an eye height of {eye} m the horizon sits about {horizon} away and is dipped {dip}° below eye level — a target can sit below 0° yet still stand above the horizon line. The “Difference” column is how much lower the globe places each target than a flat plane would — positive means the globe angle is smaller.
results-note-refr: Refraction (k = {k}) is modeled as an effective radius R_eff ≈ {reff} km, which lifts each globe angle toward the flat value.
exagg-note: ⚠ Heights and curvature exaggerated {v}× (planet drawn with radius R/{v}) — slopes and the tilt of verticals are exaggerated consistently; the printed angles are the true values.
exp1-verd: Verdict rule: if the sum comes out at 180.000° at every distance, the flat model survives and the globe is dead. If the excess grows in proportion to d, the globe survives — and dividing d by the excess gives you the Earth's radius. At d = {d} km, {detect}.
err-eye-radius: Eye height must be ≥ 0 and radius must be > 0.
err-refr-k: Refraction coefficient must be between 0 and 1.
